name: Lumen Search
blurb: A search engine and AI assistant with two billion queries a day, paid for by an ad business. Co-founder Idris Valdane still holds 25% of the vote.

directors.name: Tessa Brandt
directors.title: Attorney
directors.motive: You advise the board. If it removes him today with no written findings, the first lawsuit will ask what the cause was and your advice will be the first exhibit. You want thirty days and a law firm, and you hope to be that firm's contact.

directors.name: Priya Raman
directors.title: Labor director
directors.motive: You speak for the engineers, and most would quit if the CEO goes. You also signed the letter asking for slower releases. You oppose removal today, but you want a visible safety check that your members can see before they hear how you voted.

directors.name: Anders Lund
directors.title: Fund partner
directors.motive: Your fund owns 7% and needs December's sale at full price. You expect the technology partner to back the CEO as soon as it hears, and you promised yourself never to fire a founder again. You want him kept on a tight leash.

directors.name: Wes Calloway
directors.title: Founder's friend
directors.motive: Idris Valdane holds 25% of the vote and got you this seat. Privately he told you he will vote his shares to oust any board that fires the CEO today, but would back a thirty-day investigation. Nobody else knows this.

directors.name: Mira Castellanos
directors.title: Community seat
directors.motive: You are one of three directors who say he was not honest, and the notes on the unfinished safety review are yours. Every week he stays makes him harder to remove, but a messy firing could make safety people look reckless. You want him out.

directors.name: Raymond Osei
directors.title: Audit chair
directors.motive: You must certify the December sale and cannot sign with no findings and an undisclosed side venture. You need facts first, and the fund wants this finished today. Three new independent directors would share the weight, so you favor either route that adds them.

briefing.intro: Lumen Search runs a search engine and AI assistant with two billion queries a day. Its charter puts safe, widely shared AI ahead of profit and gives the board the final word. It is a Friday in November, the board is meeting without notice to the CEO, and a developer conference opens Monday.
facts: CEO Sam Hartigan raised the money, recruited most senior staff and drove the fastest user growth in the industry. Three directors say he was not fully honest with the board: a launch the board learned of from the press, a safety review called finished when it was not, and a side venture he did not disclose. Two of these are in emails, and one rests on a director's notes.
The board has no written findings, no law firm and no investigator. Counsel warns that the first lawsuit would ask what the cause was.

Nearly all 770 employees hold equity tied to a share sale at an $86 billion valuation in December, and many say they follow the CEO, not the board. The president will quit if the CEO goes, and a rival lab is offering to match researchers' equity.
The technology partner that supplies the computing was told nothing and could hire the CEO's team if the lab falls apart. A leak is expected within hours.

options.title: Remove the CEO now
options.text: Announce his departure today and name an interim CEO; the president, most staff and the December share sale are put at risk.

options.title: Put him on notice
options.text: Give him written expectations and a ninety-day review while he stays; the three directors who raised concerns may resign.

options.title: Investigate first
options.text: Hire an outside firm to report in thirty days and say nothing in public; leaks will fill the gap and the share sale waits.

options.title: Expand the board
options.text: Add three independent directors and move him off the board, deciding his future in spring; both camps may call it a half-measure.

reveal.text: The real firm was OpenAI. Its nonprofit board removed CEO Sam Altman in November 2023 without detailed findings. Of roughly 770 employees, 745 signed a letter threatening to leave, Microsoft offered to hire him, and he returned within days under a new board.

questions: Why did three directors distrust the CEO?
No written findings. Why does that matter?
Remove him or keep him? What tipped you?
Employees, investors, the public. Who should the board serve?

press.headline: Lumen Board Removes CEO
press.story: The board said he was not consistently honest and named the technology chief interim CEO. Safety researchers praised a board that used its charter, but the president resigned, engineers began threatening to leave, and the 25% shareholder demanded a new board.

press.headline: Lumen Board Puts CEO on Notice and Keeps Him
press.story: The CEO gets a written list of expectations and a ninety-day review. Staff were relieved, but two directors who raised the concerns resigned, and safety critics asked what had changed.

press.headline: Lumen Hires Law Firm to Investigate Its CEO
press.story: The CEO steps back from board decisions for thirty days while lawyers interview staff. The board said nothing publicly, leaks filled the gap, and the December buyer asked for a timeline.

press.headline: Lumen Adds Three Directors, Removes CEO From Board
press.story: The larger board will decide his future in spring. His closest ally on the board called it a demotion, and rival labs began calling researchers.
